# 1. Loading Data 
```{r, setup}
#| echo: FALSE

#1.2 Loading packages 
library(dplyr)
library(tidyverse)
library(glmmTMB)
library(DHARMa)
library(ggeffects)
library(emmeans)
library(broom.mixed)
library(gt)
library(AER)

#1.3 Loading the dataset
data(NMES1988)
dataset <- NMES1988

#Selecting variables from dataset
data <- dataset|>
  select(visits,
         chronic,
         health,
         gender, 
         school,
         insurance)

#Assign a reference group 
data <- data |>
  mutate(
    health = fct_relevel(factor(health), "average"),
    gender = fct_relevel(factor(gender), "male")
  )
```

## 1.2 Looking at Variables 
```{r, variable table}
#| tbl-cap: "Variable Description Table"

variable_table <- data.frame(
  Variable = c("visits", "chronic", "health", "gender", "school", "Insurance"), 
  Descprtion = c(
    "Number of physician office visits",
    "Number of chronic conditions",
    "Self-perceived health (poor, average, excellent"), 
  "Male or Female",
  "Years of education", 
  "Covered by private insurance",
  Role = c("Outcome",
           "Predictor",
           "Predictor",
           "Predictor",
           "Predictor",
           "Predictor"))
```

Our reference variable for the health category is **Average** and **Male** for the gender category. 

```{r, describe data}
#| echo: FALSE
#Describing data outcome summary 
visit_summary <- data |>
  summarise(
    n      = n(),
    mean   = mean(visits),
    var    = var(visits),
    p_zero = mean(visits == 0),
    max    = max(visits)
  )

visit_summary
```

```{r, descriptive plot}
#| echo: FALSE

# Create a plot of the overall distribution of number of visits (outcome variable)

descriptive_plot <- ggplot(data, aes(x = visits)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Physician Visits",
       x = "Number of People", 
       y = "Number of Visits in Physicians")
descriptive_plot

```
Upon initially analyzing the data, it can be observed that it is count data; all values are whole numbers being 0 or higher, and it presents a positive, right skew. The variance is `r round(visit_summary$var, 2)`) is about `r round(visit_summary$var / visit_summary$mean, 2)` times the mean (`r round(visit_summary$mean, 2)`. This data is very overdispersed and there's more spread than Poisson would assume, as Poisson assumes the variance is equal to the mean. In order to understand the count, we can see that **`r round(100 * visit_summary$p_zero)`%** have never visited the doctor. We would need to see if the model truly has this amount of zeros. 

# 2. Specify Competing Models 
## 2.1 Why not a linear model? 
```{r, gaussian model test}
#| echo: FALSE 
#| 
# Fitting a Gaussian model to see why it is not suitable for our count data 

m_gauss <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  data = data,
  family = gaussian(link = "identity"))

#simulation 
set.seed(9041)
res_gauss <- simulateResiduals(m_gauss, n = 500, plot = FALSE)
plot(res_gauss)
```
The function, DHARMa approximates new, predicted data from the fitted models and determining where the observed data is. If it was fitting the Gaussian model well, there would be uniform residuals along the QQ plot, however the shape notes that there is a cluster of low values near 0 and a cluster of higher values near 1. This linear model is not accurate predictive or representative of our count data. Deeper issues also lie, as Gaussian models can have negative counts with no bounds, however doctors visits in our data can't be less than 0. It assumes a constant variance, however the variance grows with the mean, and Poisson predicts it is the same. Finally, it treats the effects as additive, however it's more typical to multiply the count. 

## 2.2 Specifying Nested Poisson Models

We are going to specify 3 nested models here. This means that there is an intercept model with only the outcome variable, and in each model, predictors are added. 

 Model | Formula | Research rationale |
|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|
| null: Null | `visits ~ 1` | Baseline model |
| one_predictor: Chronic | `visits ~ chronic` | Evaluate number of chronic conditions |
| Full Poisson: Full | `visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance` | The remaining predictors being conditions, health status, gender, education, and insurance explain additional variation |

```{r, nested models}
#| echo: FALSE

# Null (intercept-only) Poisson model: no predictors, just the overall average.
null <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ 1, 
  data = data, 
  family = poisson(link = "log"))

# One-predictor Poisson model: does mentor productivity predict article counts?
one_predictor <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic, 
  data = data, 
  family = poisson(link = "log"))


# Full Poisson model: all five predictors at once.
poisson <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  data = data,
  family = poisson(link = "log"))
```

## 2.2 Exploring and Comparing Fitted Models 

Due to our models being nested, we can compare them all using an anova. 

```{r, anova}
#| echo: FALSE 

tests <- anova(null, one_predictor, poisson)

```

```{r, prepare tests}
#| echo: FALSE

tests <- tests |>
  select(Chisq, `Chi Df`, `Pr(>Chisq)`) |>
  rename(
    Nested.df = `Chi Df`,
    Nested.Chisq.stat = Chisq,
    Nested.p.value = `Pr(>Chisq)`)
```

### 5.2 Model Performance 


```{r, extract model metrics}
#| echo: FALSE

#Returning one row data frame 
glance0 <- broom.mixed::glance(null)
glance1 <- broom.mixed::glance(one_predictor)
glance2 <- broom.mixed::glance(poisson)
```

```{r, combine model metrics}
#| echo: FALSE

#Binding together 
mods <- c(
  "Null",
  "One_Predictor: Chronic",
  "Full")

glances <- rbind(
  glance0,
  glance1,
  glance2)
```

### 2.3 Combining Nested Test & Model Performance 

```{r, combine comparisons}
#| echo: FALSE

comparison_table <- cbind(
  Model = mods,
  glances,
  tests)
```

### 2.4 Displaying the Combined Table 

```{r, model comparison table}
#| echo: FALSE

#Creating a comparison table with important metrics 
comparison_table |>
  select(
    Model,
    AIC,
    BIC,
    logLik,
    deviance,
    df.residual,
    Nested.df,
    Nested.Chisq.stat,
    Nested.p.value
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    Model = "Model",
    AIC = "AIC",
    BIC = "BIC",
    logLik = "Log-likelihood",
    deviance = "Deviance",
    df.residual = "Residual.df",
    Nested.df = "Nested df",
    Nested.Chisq.stat = "Nested χ²",
    Nested.p.value = "Nested p"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(
      AIC,
      BIC,
      logLik,
      deviance,
      Nested.Chisq.stat
    ),
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  fmt(
    columns = Nested.p.value,
    fns = function(x) {
      ifelse(
        is.na(x),
        "—",
        ifelse(x < .001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", x))
      )
    }
  ) |>
  sub_missing(
    columns = c(Nested.df, Nested.Chisq.stat),
    missing_text = "—"
  )
```

### 2.5 Interpreting the combined table


```{r, select model}
#| echo: FALSE

selected_row <- comparison_table |>
  filter(Nested.p.value < .05) |>
  slice_tail(n = 1)

#Create an object with model's name 
selected_name <- selected_row$Model

#Case Match 
selected_model <- switch(
  selected_name,
  "Null" = null,
  "One_Predictor: Chronic" = one_predictor,
  "Full" = poisson)
```

The provisionally selected model is **`r selected_name`**, and the AIC value is **`r round(AIC(selected_model), 3)`**, and the BIC value is **`r round(BIC(selected_model), 3)`**.

# 3. Evaluating the Poisson Model 

## 3.1 Simulating Residuals 
```{r, poisson model DHARMa}
#| echo: FALSE 

#Using set.seed so that results are reproducible 
set.seed(9041)

#Simulate residuals using poisson
res_pois <- simulateResiduals(poisson, n = 500, plot = FALSE)

plot(res_pois)

```

## 3.2 Testing for Overdispersion & Excess Zeros
This test will assess whether the observed variance is larger or smaller than our Poisson model would expect, and if there are more zeros than expected. 

```{r, dispersion}
pois_disp <- testDispersion(res_pois)
pois_disp
```

```{r, zero-inflation}
pois_zeroin <- testZeroInflation(res_pois)
pois_zeroin
```

## 3.3 Interpreting the Diagnostics 

The DHARMa plots suggest that the fit of the Poisson model is less than ideal. It can be seen that in both graphs, the values on the far left being the simulated values from the model are vastly different from the red line, being the actual values. 

The dispersion ratio the plot has displayed is `r round(pois_disp$statistic, 2)` (`r ifelse(pois_disp$p.value < .001, "*p* < .001", paste0("*p* = ", round(pois_disp$p.value, 3)))`), and the expected rate of zero is `r round(pois_zeroin$statistic, 2)` times the amount of zeros that the Poisson model expects, meaning that there is a greater variance in our data than the Poisson model can account for. 

This overdispersion is important, as it carries the assumption that the variance is equal to the mean, so when this metric is incorrect, the other values that take into account the variance/mean, such as the standard errors, confidence intervals, and p-values, they are incorrect assumptions and will decrease each of these values. We cannot, however move straight to a zero-inflated model after these results, as zeros can be generated from two processes: structural (individuals never visiting the physician office), or sampling (count process, where it's sometimes zero).

# 4. Fit and Evalute Negative Binomial Model 

As the Poisson model did not fit well, we will be using a negative binomial model, which incorporates a dispersion parameter so that the variance is no longer equal to the mean. However, the Poisson model is still nested so that we can compare the two to assess which has better predictive ability (using a likelihood ratio test). 

## 4.1 Estimate the NB2 Model 
```{r, negative-binomial}
#| echo: FALSE

# Negative binomial (NB2) 
neg_binom <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  data   = data,
  family = nbinom2(link = "log"))

summary(neg_binom)
```

## 4.2 Compare the Poisson and NB2
```{r, NB vs Poisson}

#Using LRT to see if NB fits better than Poisson
lrt_nb<-anova(poisson, neg_binom)
lrt_nb
```
**DOUBLE CHECK VALUES AFTER RENDERING!**
Using a Likelihood Ratio Test to compare the Poisson model versus the negative binomial model, the χ² was found to be (`r lrt_nb[2, "Chi Df"]`) = `r round(lrt_nb[2, "Chisq"], 2)`, `r ifelse(lrt_nb[2, "Pr(>Chisq)"] < .001, "*p* < .001", paste0("*p* = ", round(lrt_nb[2, "Pr(>Chisq)"], 3)))`. These values show that the addition of another parameter (through the df value), as seen in the large Chisq value, showing that the model fits better the the added parameter. Additionally, both the AIC and BIC (**Code values**) were significantly lowered. Through these values, we can conclude that the NB2 model is a better fit. This added parameter was valuable in allowing the variance to exceed the mean, however these values cannot yet illustrate other problems such as extreme counts and excess zeros. 

## 4.3 Double-Checking NB2 with DHARMa
```{r, nb2-DHARMa}
#| echo: FALSE

#We use the same seed to be reproducible and comaprable to Poisson check. 
set.seed(9041)
res_nb <- simulateResiduals(neg_binom, n = 500, plot = FALSE)
plot(res_nb)
```

We would like to perform additional tests regarding the dispersion, as it becomes close to zero it indicates non-significance. We would also like to observe whether the model has produced a number of zeros similar to the observed, determining whether a hurdle or zero-inflated model might be needed. 
```{r, nb-tests}
#| echo: FALSE

# Dispersion test 
disp_nb <- testDispersion(res_nb)

#Production of zeros: zero-infalted or hurdle model needed?
zi_nb <- testZeroInflation(res_nb)

```

The negative binomial model has resolved overdispersion, as the ratio is now `r round(disp_nb$statistic, 2)` (`r ifelse(disp_nb$p.value < .001, "*p* < .001", paste0("*p* = ", round(disp_nb$p.value, 3)))`), and non-significant. 

### Visualizing Predicted Counts 

Coefficients on the log scale are hard to picture, so it helps to plot what the model predicts on the count scale. Here we plot predicted article counts across mentor productivity, holding the other predictors at their reference levels (Men, Single) or means (`kid5`, `phd`).

```{r nb-pred-plot}
#| echo: FALSE


#education [0:40]" plots school years from 0 to 20.
pred_nb <- predict_response(neg_binom, terms = "school [0:20]")

plot(pred_nb) +
  labs(
    title = "Predicted Physician Visits Based on Years of School",
    x = "Years of School", y = "Predicted Visits")

```
This model has created a curved line upwards, despite the predictors being linear, due to the use of a log link, as each year of school added isn't 1, but rather the log of it, multiplying the expected count. 

In double checking these plots, the QQ plots should (and are) closer to the diagonal line, in which they are, showing the NB2 is adequate with residuals being closer to predicted. However, the DHARMa residual vs predicted illustrates that there is a curve rather than the expected flat, fitted line. This curvature looks to have a pattern, meaning that the residuals likely are not random (as they should be, which would create the ideal straight line); this illustrated systemic changes, which are not desirable in a model, and they do not match the horizontal, red quantile lines. EMPHASIZE LOG LINK 

# 5. Do Zeros Need Their Own Model? 
Are there more zeros than our model predicts? 

Given our QQ plot and our residual versus predicted graph, we can see that the model gives a well-reproduced amount of zeros, and the variance is enough to account for this (observed/expected = `r round(zi_nb$statistic, 2)`, *p* = `r round(zi_nb$p.value, 3)`). Therefore, we do not need a separate model and can continue with the negative binary model. ????
rewrite to say that the zeros are underestimated, as the red line is to the right. 

*rewrite* 
The other two models that could be used are the zero-inflated model (structured versus sampling) or the hurdle model (hurdle component, and the zero-truncated component). 

```{r, zero-models}
#| echo: FALSE
#| eval: FALSE

#Here we can look at the zero-inflated model and the hurdle model

# Zero-inflated model with constant zero 
m_zinb <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  ziformula = ~ 1,
  data = data, family = nbinom2()
)

# Zero-inflated NB with predictors in zero
m_zinb_full <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  ziformula = ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  data = data, family = nbinom2()
)

# Hurdle Model 
m_hurd <- glmmTMB(
 visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  ziformula = ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  data = data, family = truncated_nbinom2()
 )

# Comparing hurdle and zero models
anova(neg_binom, m_zinb_full)

# As they are not nested, we must use AIC and not BIC 
AIC(neg_binom, m_zinb, m_zinb_full, m_hurd)
BIC(neg_binom, m_zinb, m_zinb_full, m_hurd)

# Double checking the models with DHARMa
set.seed(9041)
res_hurd <- simulateResiduals(m_hurd, n = 500, plot = FALSE)
testZeroInflation(res_hurd)
```
Upon using the hurdle and zero-inflated models, there are interesting findings. The NB2 and ZINB showed that the LRT value of the ZINB was higher than that of NB2 (as they were nested models), showing the added complexity was worth it, as it is better fitting. As NB2, ZINB and hurdle models are not nested, they must be compared with AIC and BIC metrics. It was shown that *inline code for all 3*, showing that values for NM2 are the highest, followed by ZINB, then hurdle model values being the smallest, showing that it has the best predictive accuracy. Upon double checking the chosen, hurdle model, it is seen that the observed values are very well within the estimated values, supporting its ability as a model. For these aforementioned reasons, I chose to continue with the hurdle model.
